title: Greetings and Introductions in Healthcare Settings
description: Master essential greetings and self-introductions for professional healthcare environments

canDoStatements: I can greet patients and colleagues appropriately in formal and informal situations
I can introduce myself and state my role in a healthcare setting
I can ask someone's name and understand their response
I can use polite expressions like 'please', 'thank you', and 'excuse me'
I can distinguish between formal (Sie) and informal (du) address
focusAreas: Basic greeting vocabulary (Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend)
Formal vs. informal address (Sie vs. du)

scenario.title: First Day at the Hospital
scenario.context: You are a newly hired nurse at a German hospital. Today is your first day, and you need to introduce yourself to colleagues and patients. You'll meet the head nurse, greet patients during morning rounds, and interact with doctors and other staff.
scenario.realWorldApplication: These phrases are essential for daily interactions in any German healthcare facility. Proper greetings set a professional tone and help build trust with patients.
culturalNotes: Germans value formality in professional settings - always use 'Sie' with patients and new colleagues
A firm handshake and direct eye contact are expected when introducing yourself
Use academic titles (Dr., Professor) when addressing doctors
Morning greetings are important - always greet colleagues when arriving at work

survivalPhrases.german: Guten Morgen! Ich bin die neue Krankenschwester.
survivalPhrases.english: Good morning! I am the new nurse.
survivalPhrases.pronunciation: GOO-ten MOR-gen! Ikh bin dee NOY-eh KRAN-ken-shves-ter.
survivalPhrases.usage: Use when introducing yourself to colleagues on your first day
Essential phrase for checking on patients during rounds
Offer assistance to patients or visitors
When you need a moment to attend to something

survivalPhrases.english: Excuse me, what is your name?

items.english: Thank you / Thank you very much

generalVocab.exampleTranslation: I am called Maria. / My name is Maria.

healthcareVocab.exampleTranslation: The male nurse works in the hospital.

healthcareVocab.note: Note the umlaut in plural: Ärzte

grammar.title: Formal vs. Informal Address (Sie vs. du)
grammar.explanation: German has two ways to say 'you': formal (Sie) and informal (du). In healthcare, ALWAYS use 'Sie' with patients and colleagues you don't know well.
rules: Use 'Sie' (formal) with: patients, supervisors, doctors, new colleagues, anyone in professional settings
Use 'du' (informal) with: close friends, family, children under 16, colleagues who have agreed to use 'du'
'Sie' is always capitalized, even in the middle of a sentence
The verb form for 'Sie' is the same as the plural 'sie' (they) and 'wir' (we) forms

examples.usage: Use with patients and professional contacts
Use only with close friends or children

practiceExercises: Decide: Use 'Sie' or 'du' when speaking to a patient?
Decide: Use 'Sie' or 'du' when speaking to the hospital director?

grammar.title: The Verb 'heißen' (to be called)
grammar.explanation: 'heißen' is used to state names. It literally means 'to be called' and is essential for introductions.

examples.english: His name is Thomas. / He is called Thomas.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich bin Anna. (literal: I am Anna)
commonMistakes.note: While 'Ich bin Anna' is understood, 'Ich heiße Anna' is more natural for stating your name

grammar.title: German Articles and Gender
grammar.explanation: All German nouns have a gender (masculine, feminine, or neuter) and require an article. Learning the article with each noun is essential.

examples.tip: Most male occupations and male people are masculine
Most female occupations and female people are feminine
Many buildings and facilities are neuter

learningStrategies: Always learn the article WITH the noun - never learn a noun alone
Use color-coding: blue for der (masculine), red for die (feminine), green for das (neuter)
Look for patterns: -ung, -heit, -keit endings are usually feminine
Compound nouns take the gender of the last word: Kranken+haus → das Haus → das Krankenhaus

dialogues.title: Meeting a Patient for the First Time
dialogues.scenario: You enter a patient's room during morning rounds

lines.speaker: Nurse (You)
lines.german: Guten Morgen! Ich bin Krankenschwester Anna.
lines.english: Good morning! I am Nurse Anna.

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.english: My name is Schmidt. Peter Schmidt.

lines.speaker: Nurse (You)
lines.german: Sehr erfreut, Herr Schmidt. Wie geht es Ihnen heute?
lines.english: Very pleased to meet you, Mr. Schmidt. How are you feeling today?

vocabulary: Wie heißen Sie? - What is your name?
Sehr erfreut - Very pleased to meet you
Wie geht es Ihnen? - How are you?
culturalNotes: Always use titles (Herr/Frau) with last names in professional settings
Wait for the patient to respond before asking about their condition
A polite greeting sets a positive tone for care

dialogues.title: Introducing Yourself to a Colleague
dialogues.scenario: First day at work, meeting the head nurse

lines.speaker: You
lines.german: Guten Tag! Ich bin neu hier. Ich heiße Anna Müller.
lines.english: Good day! I am new here. My name is Anna Müller.

lines.speaker: Head Nurse
lines.german: Guten Tag, Frau Müller. Willkommen! Ich bin die Stationsleiterin, Frau Weber.
lines.english: Good day, Ms. Müller. Welcome! I am the head nurse, Ms. Weber.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Very pleased to meet you, Ms. Weber.

exercises.title: Listen and Identify
exercises.instructions: Listen to each greeting and identify the time of day

questions.question: What time of day is this greeting used?
questions.explanation: 'Guten Morgen' is used in the morning, typically until around 11 AM.

questions.question: What time of day is this greeting used?
questions.explanation: 'Guten Abend' is used in the evening, typically after 6 PM.

exercises.title: Complete the Conversation
exercises.instructions: Fill in the blanks with the correct German words

questions.question: Guten Morgen! _____ heiße Anna. (My name is Anna)
questions.explanation: 'Ich' means 'I' in German. 'Ich heiße Anna' = 'My name is Anna'

questions.question: _____ heißen Sie? (What is your name?)
questions.explanation: 'Wie heißen Sie?' is how you ask someone's name formally. 'Wie' means 'how/what'

questions.question: Ich bin die neue _____. (I am the new nurse)
_____ Tag! (Good afternoon!)
questions.explanation: 'Guten Tag' is the standard greeting for 'Good day/afternoon'

exercises.instructions: Match each German phrase with its English translation

exercises.title: Formal or Informal?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether to use formal (Sie) or informal (du) in each situation

questions.question: You are speaking to a patient in the hospital. Which form should you use?
questions.explanation: Always use 'Sie' (formal) with patients in professional healthcare settings

questions.question: You are speaking to the hospital director. Which form should you use?
questions.explanation: Always use 'Sie' (formal) with superiors and professional contacts

questions.question: You are speaking to a child patient (age 10). Which form should you use?
questions.explanation: Use 'du' (informal) with children under 16 years old

questions.question: You are speaking to a new colleague on your first day. Which form should you use?
questions.explanation: Start with 'Sie' (formal) with new colleagues. They may later invite you to use 'du'

exercises.instructions: You will practice introducing yourself to a patient. Record or speak your responses.
exercises.scenario: You enter Mr. Hoffmann's room for the first time during morning rounds.

exchanges.prompt: The patient looks at you. What do you say?
exchanges.expectedResponse: Guten Morgen! Ich bin Krankenschwester [Your Name].

exchanges.prompt: How do you ask the patient's name?
How do you respond politely and ask how they're feeling?
exchanges.expectedResponse: Sehr erfreut, Herr Hoffmann. Wie geht es Ihnen heute?

exercises.title: Pronunciation Practice
exercises.instructions: Listen and repeat each phrase. Pay attention to the sounds.

tips: The 'u' in 'Guten' is pronounced like 'oo' in 'book'
The 'g' at the end of 'Morgen' is softened, almost like a 'k' sound
Stress is on the first syllable: KRAN-
